fields: Block (window) length for the overdispersion test: number of consecutive CpGs grouped before computing clumping
The number of consecutive CpGs that make up one block ('the globe's regions') over which the C-Score's clumping statistic is computed; set to 1,000 CpGs.

It sets the block length over which the C-Score (instrument 11) sums each tile's squared excess of held errors over its own prediction, divided by the binomial variance, to test whether excess discordance is even or clumped along the genome.

The C-Score needs a defined stretch of genome ('the blocks clumping is measured over') to sum per-tile squared departures into a single per-block statistic; without a fixed region size there is no consistent window for that sum.

record.link: 11. IAM-A C-Score (molecules: clumping of held errors)

fields: IAM-A C-Score on the globe (also called '11. IAM-A C-Score (molecules: clumping of held errors)')
Overdispersion of discordance along the genome: clumped or even (a dispersion index; 1 = independent)

Clumping of held errors over the globe's regions: whether each type's excess held error is even across the genome or clumped (a dispersion index; independent errors give 1). As currently run, it uses one pooled held error for all ~20,000 regions and mostly measures ordinary healthy differences between regions (test value C = 2.1657; no healthy band yet).

It tests whether each type's excess of held errors is even across the genome or clumped, by comparing the squared excess of held errors over each tile's own prediction against the binomial variance, per block of consecutive tiles; independent errors give 1.
An excess of held errors spread evenly across the genome is a different finding from the same excess clumped into particular regions; this reading tells them apart.
How it is obtained or computed

Per block of consecutive tiles, take the squared excess of held errors over each tile's own prediction, divided by the binomial variance; independent errors give 1. As run, it currently uses one pooled held error for all ~20,000 regions, giving C = 2.1657 (test_path: development.genome_globe.iama_cscore.C; basis: statistics).
Computed per block of consecutive tiles across the genome, pooled over roughly 20,000 regions (development.genome_globe.iama_cscore.C); not a single-locus reading.

Its law_part is IAM's Law, link 1d, long form section 1d ('the hold is the same rule, slow: the slow-write rule'). That section derives held/lost = (x/2)/(1-(1-e^{-x})/x) for a slow write, with the cell's restore at x = w = 2M = 41.9, giving odds 21.45, E_hold = 3.066 kT, and phi = 0.1464 ≈ ln M/M. Status given for that link: 'identity confirmed symbolically on GitHub (run 44662887227; sudden limit odds = 1)'; open item noted there is that the horizon's held share of 1 as the adiabatic limit (x→∞) still needs its own mapping of x.

Design finding 11-20: C = 2.17 uses ONE pooled held error for all ~20,000 regions; the null spread is sqrt(2/20147) = 0.010, so C mostly measures ordinary healthy differences between regions rather than true clumping (the statistic's own docstring calls this 'clustering, or healthy differences between regions'). Two fixes are proposed but not yet done: Fix 1, save region counts in the bundle so a band can come from the atlas libraries in the full run; Fix 2, score each region against its own expected held error from IAM-A's line at that region's loose share (self-reference, no atlas), keeping the pooled form beside it.

fields: Over the sequencing globe's regions (1,000 consecutive CpGs, at least 200 chances each): C = sum over regions of (observed held errors - predicted)^2 / sum of the binomial variance, the prediction for each region from the sample's own IAM-A line at that region's loose share. Independent errors give 1; above 1 the excess is clumped in some regions.
A sample-wide IAM-A can rise because every region loses a little or because a few regions lose a lot; the second is the signature of local failure (and the base for a regional 'where').

questions: Why per region and not just one number?
One number cannot tell many small losses from a few large ones; the dispersion across regions can.
